reviewer: Claude agent review (Fable 5.1), not a human historian
text: 2026-10-10: approved on the third full read of story.json after two rounds of blockers. The first pass found four text blockers and no image blockers; the second pass found that three of the four paragraph fixes had not landed and that the owner had meanwhile redesigned the lead and replaced seven pictures; the third pass verified every fix by grep on the current file. This approval binds the text and the thirteen pictures as they stand after those edits.

Read the whole story.json (introduction, twelve scenes with titles, alt texts and dramatised lists, summary, didYouKnow, visitToday, provenance, illustration disclosure, content note) against facts.json, research/ganga.md and research/ganga-verified.md (verbatim Rice 1889 EC II nos. 38, 67, 75-76, 89, 109 and Introduction pp. 22-35; Narasimhachar 1923 nos. 59, 121, 133, 175-180, 281 and Introduction pp. 44-47; Hultzsch EI VII pp. 108-110; Buchanan 1807 vol. III pp. 410-411; Rice's summaries of the Bhujabali Charita, the Rajavali Kathe and Mackenzie). Every event, name, place, number and year traces to a fact id cited by its scene; invented texture (the night camp and the cup on the rock, the fast inside the basadi, the throne hall, the writing desk with Nemichandra in the room, the two bard scenes, the scaffolds and the masons' numbers, the minister watching the lines cut, the pillar carved beside the statue, the basadi being topped out, Gangaraja watching, Buchanan's work described, all dialogue) is named in each scene's dramatised list.

Blockers fixed before approval: scene-02 called Indra IV the grandson of Marasimha's 'friend', which no source says; he is now ತನ್ನ ಸಹೋದರಿಯ ಮಗ, ಚಕ್ರವರ್ತಿ ಮೂರನೇ ಕೃಷ್ಣನ ಮೊಮ್ಮಗ (1923 no. 133: son's son of Krishna III, daughter's son of Butuga, who was Marasimha's father). Scene-10 stated as record that Chavundaraya died before his basadi was finished and that the son built it in his memory; both are Rice's 'it would appear' (Intro pp. 34-35) and the 1923 edition also credits the basti to Chavundaraya himself (no. 122), so the text now says ರೈಸ್ ಊಹಿಸಿದರು, the summary says only what no. 67 says (ಮಾಡಿಸಿದ), and the dramatised note adds that the basadi beginning in his lifetime is inference. Scene-03 called Rachamalla ಯುವಕ with no record of his age; now ಹೊಸ ರಾಜ with the youth disclosed as the picture's invention. Scene-08 said tenth-century stones call the image Gommata; no tenth-century inscription read names it, the tenth-century witness is the Gommatasara, so the text and f-bahubali-later now say ಹತ್ತನೇ ಶತಮಾನದ ಗೊಮ್ಮಟಸಾರ ಮತ್ತು ನಂತರದ ಕಲ್ಲುಗಳು and that the name is first on stone in the twelfth century.

Nits fixed on the same passes: the palm-leaf stylus ಕಂಟ (was ಕಂಠ, throat) in scene-04 text and alt; 'by order of Indra' kept as ರಾಷ್ಟ್ರಕೂಟ ಇಂದ್ರನ ಆಜ್ಞೆಯಂತೆ; the Brahma-Kshatra gloss separated from what the pillar says; the Rachamalla link credited to the later stones (text and f-rachamalla) since no. 109 names no Rachamalla; the Uchchangi 'never taken' line now cites f-marasimha-epitaph; the Purana's audience gloss dropped; 'several titles are not of war'; Rice's silence argument told as his (ರೈಸ್ ಪ್ರಕಾರ); the merchant at the king's court; Rice reported the metre scale rather than measured it; the Arittonemi record moved back ಎಂಟು ದಶಕ; the signature lines placed beside the legs under the hands; Hultzsch's 'probably' kept for the Tamil line; the Tyagada pillar ಎರಡೂ ಕಾಲು ಮೀಟರ್; the name Gullakayajji marked as modern (Rice: Kushmandini); the bard's pond sentence reworded; the 995 line on the old image in the later upper storey; Gangaraja's enclosure as the first form of today's; his poets chose the comparison; dandanayaka added to f-gangaraja; Scanlon of the Public Works Department; 144 inscriptions of Shravanabelagola; the lines read 'not correctly' rather than 'by nobody'; the scene-01 and scene-05 dramatised notes name the 1923 reading of the Vajvala rout and the composite legend; ದಪ್ಪ replaced by ಎತ್ತರದ after the redesign.

Quotations and close paraphrases compared with the verbatim texts: no. 109 (Brahma-Kshatra race, Vajvala's army fleeing like deer by order of Indra before Jagadekavira, the black serpent my arrow, Chaladanka-Ganga's design rendered vain, the jewelled skull-cups brimming with heroes' blood); no. 38 (the Pallava skulls and the Kapalika, the places fought, Chera Chola Pandya Pallava, one year more, Ajitasena-bhattaraka of Bankapura, the three-day vow of the 1923 reading, the Chola and Pandya verse); the Purana titles and Rice's 'no mention of a single work of religious merit... warfare and bloodshed from beginning to end' and 'incredible that so great a work should have been unnoticed'; Rice on the lines 'original grandeur of their simplicity' and 'the bold sculptor... not so much as left a record of his name'; Rice's description of the colossus and the scale of 3 ft 3 1/2 in, the French metre; nos. 75-76 in Hultzsch's readings (Sri Chamundaraja madisidam; Sri Chamundarajan seyvittan in Grantha and Vatteluttu; Sri Chavundaraje karaviyale; Sri Gangaraja suttalayavam madisidam) with the sides as Rice gives them; Hultzsch's Marathi, the pilgrims from the Maratha country and the identical letter-type of the two Nagari lines; no. 67 'the minister Chamunda's son had this home for Jina made, the lay-disciple of Ajitasena' with Jinadevana from the 1923 Introduction; no. 89 'Raya, the minister of king Racha-Malla'; 'a hundred-fold more fortunate than the former Raya of the Gangas'; 1923 no. 133 on Indra IV's polo and his 982 sallekhana; Buchanan's 120 houses, the inflammation of the eyes, 70 ft 3 in, 'for the accuracy of which I cannot answer', Wellesley's two remarks, 'a certain Chamunda Raya, descended from whom were the nine Belalla Rajas'; Scanlon's 50 ft, 9 ft, 26 ft and the priests interfering, Rice's 57 ft; Rice's rejection of Gomates of Behistun. The legends follow Rice's summaries of the Bhujabali Charita (merchant, 525 bow-lengths, Kalikambe, the milk vow), the Rajavali Kathe (Padmavati, the arrow south from the smaller hill, thirteen men high, the navel, the gullakayi shell, Belgola) and Mackenzie, and the text says the bard tells them as one; the 'golden' arrow and the name Gullakayajji are marked as modern; the 1231 Yakshi of Bammi-setti and the 18th-century tank are stated.

Disputed points stated as disputed in the text and in bilingual disputed notes: who Jagadekavira is (Marasimha for Rice and Hultzsch, Rachamalla for Narasimhachar); who killed Nagavarma (both readings given, fratricide not asserted); Marasimha's death 974 or 975; Rachamalla's number and reign; the colossus 981 or 983; the Nagari line of Chavundaraya's time or of 1116; the Vaddaradhane's date behind 'earliest dated prose'; the Tyagada relief as a portrait; the Arittonemi guess abandoned; the unrecorded death; the end of the Gangas c. 1000. Years appear only where the records are dated (973, c. 974, 978, 981 or 983, 982, c. 985, c. 995, c. 1116, c. 1231, 1800, 1871, 1889) and the bard scenes carry none.

Genealogy and numbers checked: Marasimha son of Butuga; Indra IV grandson of Krishna III and Marasimha's sister's son; Rachamalla IV Marasimha's successor; Nagavarma younger brother; Pullabba sister; Jinadevana son; Gangaraja minister of Vishnuvardhana; Hulla of Narasimha; 57 feet; 113 lines on three faces plus Kannada on the fourth; Saka 900; 144 inscriptions; twelve-year anointing. Chavundaraya's name is spelt ಚಾವುಂಡರಾಯ throughout and ಚಾಮುಂಡರಾಜ only where the stone has it.

Kannada: told-story register for adults, no vulgarity; no em dash anywhere; NFC; no OCR debris; the skull-cups, the sallekhana deaths, the nude monks and the nude image are covered by the content note, which is truthful. kn and en alt texts and the disclosure agree.

story.facts is byte-identical to facts.json (33 facts); every scene and didYouKnow id resolves and every fact is used; tiers: inscription for nos. 38, 67, 75-76, 89, 109, 133, the Purana colophon and Buchanan, scholarship for the datings, Rice's descriptions, the name Gommata, Pullabba, the measurements and the two visual rules, legend for the three legend facts; mixed facts carry disputed notes separating record from inference.
illustrations: All thirteen WebPs (cover, scene-01 to scene-12, 1600x900) were opened and compared with their scene paragraphs, alt texts and bible/style.md, with enlarged crops of hands, forts, horses, palm leaf, both rock faces, far hills, scaffolds and the village. The owner rejected the first heavy-built design of Chavundaraya; he was redesigned as a tall, strong general with a square jaw, thick moustache, no beard, hair in a knot, grey at the temples and a scar on the left forearm, and seven pictures were replaced (cover, scene-01, scene-03, scene-04, scene-06, scene-07, scene-08); bible/style.md was updated to the new look and the word ದಪ್ಪ removed from the text. The seven replacements were reopened and re-checked; this approval hashes the replaced files.
No image blockers in either set. The first set's only period fault, scene-01's fort as an ashlar castle with square towers, went away with the replacement, which shows rubble walls on a crag.

cover: the general in his fifties at the lotus pedestal, white fillet with upright plume, moustache, scar, straight sword, white dhoti with red border; the colossus's feet, creeper and cobras rising out of frame; a monk seated in a rock shadow in side view with a pichchi; Chandragiri with small shrines and the village across the valley. Nit: the far shrines have small tiered towers and no anthills show round the legs.

scene-01: night camp below a burning rubble hill fort; the general with sword and dagger, the jewelled cup on the rock; elephants in plain cloth, a horse with a cloth saddle and no stirrup, round shields, spears, tents. Clean.
scene-02: thin bearded king in white with the crown on the floor, a monk on a stone bench in side view with a pichchi, guards at a distance, a pillar being raised outside by a timber derrick. Clean.

scene-03: timber court by the river; the young crowned king in pearls; the general with one hand on the throne and one on a straight sword; the Ganga elephant on a red cloth banner; chowrie women; bowing chiefs; a guard in a gold-banded head-wrap. Clean.

scene-04: lamp-lit night, the general greying at the temples incising a palm leaf with a stylus, sword on a cloth, a monk seated in back view in shadow, a moonlit hill in the window. Nit: the leaf carries AI pseudo-strokes, not readable script.

scene-05: white-bearded bard with a drum on Chandragiri's steps, pilgrims, the small colossus silhouette on Vindhyagiri at sunset, village of tiled and thatched houses. Clean for a sixteenth-century frame.

scene-06: head and shoulders of the colossus emerging among rope-lashed timber scaffolds, ringlet hair, long ears, half-open eyes, faint smile, creeper on the arm; masons tiny against it; the minister and a nude monk seen from behind. Nit: small towered shrines on Chandragiri in a tenth-century frame.

scene-07: feet and lotus pedestal; a mason with mallet and chisel over a chalk guide-line and chips, no letters; the minister with folded arms. Nit: the line is cut on the rock below the pedestal rather than on the anthill rock below the hands.

scene-08: the Tyagada pillar base relief of a plumed seated man and a seated monk being carved; the minister on a stone bench, the monk with palm leaves in side view, two chowrie women; the colossus's feet behind. Clean.

scene-09: night, the bard with drum by a lamp, an old woman with a gourd, a natural moonlit pond between the hills, Chandragiri shrines, a village of oil lamps. Clean; the pond is not the eighteenth-century stepped tank.

scene-10: a plain granite basadi being topped out with a pulley derrick, a young man in white at the door, a monk in the doorway shadow, small tiered basadis and a manastambha with a pavilion top, Vindhyagiri with the colossus far off. Clean.

scene-11: a bearded jewelled Hoysala minister, a mason cutting rows of abstract pecking on a rock face, workers raising masonry round the colossus, bullock carts. Nits: the enclosure is drawn as a stepped block mass against the statue rather than a cloister wall round it; the line is cut on a cliff away from the statue.

scene-12: present-day Mahamastakabhisheka, priests in white pouring milk from a steel-and-timber scaffold, streams down the whole figure, a crowd with marigolds and saffron. Nit: today's enclosure walls and mantapa are absent.

No image shows a helmet, mail, a curved sword, a stirrup, a Mughal turban, a lion, boar or gandabherunda emblem, a Hoysala or Vijayanagara temple at close range, an enclosure wall before 1116, the stepped tank, modern letters on stone, or close frontal nudity; the colossus is shown feet-only, waist-up, or full-length at a distance with the crowd masking the lower half, and the monks are seated in side or back view; the general is the same man in all seven pictures that show him; no extra hands or fingers were found.
limitations: This is an AI review by a Claude agent; no human historian or epigraphist has read the text or checked the images.

Fact checking was limited to the research files in data/history-src/research (Rice 1889 archive.org djvu text, Narasimhachar 1923 page images, Hultzsch EI VII page text, Buchanan 1807 djvu text, Fleet EI VI transcription) and did not re-fetch the primary sources; the 1923 translations of nos. 121 and 122, the Bhujabali Charita's edition, the Rajavali Kathe's Kannada text, Asiatic Researches IX and Indian Antiquary II were not read at first hand by anyone on this project.

Pullabba's sallekhana, the name Gommata as the minister's pet name, the Tyagada relief's identification and its c. 983 date, the Bankapura coronation site, the 1004 end of the Gangas and the 981 computation rest on Nagarajaiah, Sarma, Krishna Rao, Kamath and popular datings as reported in the research, not on a primary text read here; the Chavundaraya Purana itself was not read.

No portrait of Chavundaraya survives; his face, the faces of every other person, the camp, the court, the writing room and the tenth-century buildings are invented, as the disclosure says. The colossus is a re-imagining from Rice's description and the Commons photographs, not a photograph.

Small far-distance details could not be verified individually: the shrines on Chandragiri and in the plain in the cover and scene-06 look slightly towered for the tenth century; scene-07 and scene-11 place the signature lines on the wrong part of the rock; scene-11's enclosure is drawn as a masonry mass; scene-12 lacks today's enclosure. These are recorded as nits and were not regenerated.

The images were judged at 1600x900 WebP with enlarged crops; the pseudo-strokes on scene-04's palm leaf and the pecked rows on scene-11's rock are not readable text and must not be taken as renderings of any inscription.
